'''Yameo''' is an extinct language of the [[Peba–Yaguan languages|Peba–Yaguan language family]] formerly spoken along the banks of the [[Amazon River]] from the [[Tigre River]] to the [[Nanay River]] in [[Peru]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rivet |first=Paul |date=1911 |title=La famille linguistique Peba |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/jsa_0037-9174_1911_num_8_1_3731 |journal=Journal de la société des américanistes |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=173–206 |doi=10.3406/jsa.1911.3731}}</ref>

Masamae (Mazán, Parara), spoken around the [[Mazán District|Mazán]] River in [[Loreto Department]], Peru,<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles |url-access=registration |authorlink=Čestmír Loukotka}}</ref> is an alternative name of the Yameo language.<ref>{{Glottolog|yame1242|Yameo|5.3|2026}}</ref>

==Name==
[[Günter Tessmann]] (1930) reports the [[Yameo]] called themselves {{Lang|yme|yameo}}, a term of uncertain origin, though Lucas Espinoza Pérez (1955) reported that this term was no longer in use in [[San Francisco de Regis]], its residents referring to themselves as {{Lang|es|san reginos}}, but some people remembered it.<ref name=":0">{{Cite thesis |last=Peña |first=Jaime G. |title=A historical reconstruction of the Peba-Yaguan linguistic family |date=2009 |degree=masters |publisher=Eugene: University of Oregon |url=https://scholarsbank.uoregon.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/ed23210d-7268-45d2-ab67-b8b42c896461/content}}</ref>

== Geographical distribution ==
The Yameo were distributed between the lower [[Tigre River|Tigre]] and [[Napo River|Napo Rivers]]. The Yameo lived in forests and ravines surrounding the smaller [[Curaray River|Curaray]], [[Mazan River|Mazan]], [[Nahuapo River|Nahuapo]], [[Nanay River|Nanay]], and [[Itaya River|Itaya Rivers]]. To their west were the [[Urarina|Itucale]], who spoke the [[language isolate]] [[Urarina language|Urarina]]; to their north were the [[Zaparoan languages|Zaparoan]]-speaking [[Semigae]], [[Sápara|Zaparo]], and [[Iquito language|Iquito]]; to their east were the {{ill|Maijuna|lt=Payagua|es|Maijuna}}, [[Matsés]], and further some Peban groups, including the Caumari; finally, to their south were the [[Kokama people|Cocama]] and [[Omagua people|Omagua]].<ref name=":0" />

==Dialects==
[[John Alden Mason]] (1950) subdivides Yameo into the ''Napeano, Masamai, Nahuapo, Amaona, Mikeano, Parrano, Yarrapo, Alabono, San Regino (?), Mazan (?),'' and ''Camuchivo (?)'' groups.<ref name="Mason-1950">{{cite book |last=Mason |first=John Alden |authorlink=John Alden Mason |date=1950 |chapter=The languages of South America |editor-first1=Julian |editor-last1=Steward |title=Handbook of South American Indians |volume=6 |pages=157–317 |publisher=[[Smithsonian Institution]], [[Bureau of American Ethnology]] Bulletin 143 |location=Washington, D.C., Government Printing Office}}</ref>

== History ==
By 1925, the Yameo language had been reduced to three speakers, according to Tessmann, the rest having adopted [[Cocama language|Cocama]], [[Quechuan languages|Quechua]], or Spanish.<ref>{{Cite book |date=1948 |title=Handbook of South American Indians: Volume 3 The Tropical Forest Tribes |url=https://hdl.handle.net/10088/34599 |language=en|last=Steward|first=Julian H.|editor-last=Steward|editor-first=Julian H.|last2=Métraux|author-link2=Alfred Métraux|first2=Alfred|chapter=The Peban Tribes|publisher=[[Smithsonian Institution]], [[Bureau of American Ethnology]] Bulletin 143 |location=Washington, D.C., Government Printing Office}}</ref>
